items.content:
Where has our profit 💸 gone?
.
.
.
I recently spoke with a manufacturing business owner who told me:

"Our turnover is good, but there is less money left at the end of the month. I am having to deal with price increases every day".

In many manufacturing businesses, profit doesn't disappear overnight, but it can leak away through:

• Supplier price increases that have not been effectively challenged
• Poor stock control practices 🚽 
• Inefficient production processes 🚽 
• Unnecessary overtime 📈 
• Mis-calculated customer pricing 💷 that no longer reflects true costs
• Duplicated effort and rework
• Waste 🚽 

What many businesses don't know is where the leaks are and why they are occurring, but they do know the bank account doesn't look as healthy 🤒 as it could.

A common reaction is to apply pressure to the sales team, however it is often worth asking:

"Are we retaining enough profit from the sales we already have?"

Over the years, I have found that most manufacturing businesses have far more improvement opportunities than they realise. The challenge is knowing where to look 👓 and engaging the team to root out and resolve the issues.

Sometimes the biggest growth opportunity isn't more revenue, it's stopping the profit leakage.
…
If you suspect profit is leaking 😢 from your business but cannot identify exactly from where, an independent structured business performance review can often reveal opportunities that have been hiding in plain sight. 

DM me so I may help you and your business.

items.content:
Lately, I'm getting pulled into many conversations about Artificial Intelligence in supply chains. You probably are, too.

Many of the leaders I've spoken with are looking for "quick wins" and "low-hanging fruit" by implementing AI... somewhere. Anywhere. Maybe it's procurement, maybe it's transportation, maybe it's labor management, etc.

I see two major risks here:

1) Opportunity cost. By choosing a quick win, we may ignore options that could create more value.

2) Amplification of dysfunction. If the current process is broken, adding AI can accelerate the destruction of value.

A better strategy is to look across the supply chain to identify the places where AI can truly complete tasks better, faster, and cheaper than humans. And, perhaps, where AI allows you to re-engineer your processes altogether.

In order to do that, you need to start by understanding the wide range of (often disconnected) information systems that are already in use by companies who work in manufacturing, retail, and distribution.

That's what this course was designed to do: Supply Chain Beyond the Basics: Leveraging Supply Chain Information Systems. 

Check it out on LinkedIn Learning! I have made it free for you with the link below.

~Mr. Supply Chain®

items.content:
Last weekend, I had the pleasure of having dinner at Titash Restaurant in Rugby, England with Richard Wilding OBE  (Professor), Dr. Muddassir Ahmed, and Sean Culey.

This week, as I've been traveling across the United States, I've been listening to the audiobook of Sean's book, "Transition Point."

I read the book when it was first published in 2018. Revisiting it now, I have an entirely new appreciation for just how insightful Sean's thinking was. 

The book was written before COVID-19 reshaped global supply chains. It was written before generative AI and ChatGPT entered the mainstream. Yet it remarkably explains many of the forces that have shaped, and continue to shape, our economy and our supply chains. Or, as Sean might say, the journey from Steam Engines to Search Engines.

What strikes me most is how well the book connects technology, economics, complexity, and human behavior into a coherent picture of the world we're living in today.

Some of the themes that continue to resonate include:

▶ The transition from the Industrial Age to a new era driven by data, networks, and intelligence.
▶ Why exponential technologies create nonlinear change that traditional management approaches struggle to address.
▶ How increasing complexity makes prediction more difficult and adaptability more valuable.
▶ Why organizations must shift from optimizing individual functions to thinking in terms of interconnected systems.
▶ The growing importance of resilience, collaboration, and trust over efficiency alone.
▶ How emerging technologies should augment human decision making rather than simply automate existing processes.

As someone who spends a great deal of time thinking and writing about Supply Chain 5.0, I have to acknowledge that many of the ideas I've been exploring are anticipated in this book.

If you want to understand the bigger picture behind what's happening in today's supply chains, I would consider Transition Point required reading.

Have you read it? If so, I'd love to hear what ideas have stayed with you.

~Mr. Supply Chain®

#AlwaysBeLearning #SupplyChain #SupplyChain5_0

P.S. I can highly recommend the "Prof Richard's Curry" from the Titash menu!

The latest edition of Supply Chained is now available.

When most people think about supply chain innovation, they think about AI, robotics, or automation. But one of the most important transformations underway is happening inside the humble shipping container.

In this issue, I sit down with Dr. Marianna Levtov to discuss:
▶ The rise of smart containers and IoT-enabled visibility
▶ Why standards and "industrial diplomacy" matter as much as technology
▶ The debate over data ownership, monetization, governance, and quality
▶ Why critical safety data should transcend commercial boundaries
▶ The connection between smart containers, the Physical Internet, and Supply Chain 5.0
▶ How resilience, sustainability, and human-centricity depend on better information sharing

One of the most interesting parts of the conversation builds on a discussion Marianna, Bart A. De Muynck, and I had during our session at TPM26. As supply chains become increasingly connected, the question is no longer whether we can collect data. The real questions are who owns it, who can access it, how it should be governed, and whether it can be trusted.
The sensors exist. The networks exist. The data exists.

The future challenge is transforming that information into coordinated action across increasingly complex supply chain ecosystems.

Thank you, Marianna, for a fascinating conversation and for the important work you are doing to help shape the future of supply chain visibility.

~Mr. Supply Chain®

#AlwaysBeLearning #SupplyChain #SupplyChain5_0

If the ASCM Board is looking for continuity rather than transformation in its next CEO, SCM professionals should pay close attention.

A conservative, certification-focused strategy might protect the past — but it won't build the future.

The likely result: flat growth, followed by a slow decline in relevance and demand.

Why should you care?

Because your career cannot rely solely on credentials.

APICS certifications still matter. They provide credibility, structure, and foundational knowledge.

But employers need more than just certified professionals. They need capable professionals who can solve problems, make decisions, explain trade-offs, and deliver measurable results.

Knowing the formula is not enough.

Can you use it to improve forecast accuracy, reduce inventory risk, challenge supplier assumptions, or defend service-level decisions?

That is where capability makes a difference.

Certification gets attention, but very little these days from most SCM organizations and professionals. Less than 3% of LinkedIn job postings require or prefer ASCM Certifications.

✈️ The data-center construction boom is lifting airfreight demand.

Companies are paying a premium to fly in supplies like power racks and semiconductors from Asia rather than wait for slower, cheaper ocean transport to fuel the rapid pace of data-center construction across the U.S.

The activity comes as higher U.S. tariffs eat into the market for cheap e-commerce packages from the likes of Shein and Temu that had flooded freight networks over the past several years.

“The airfreight market seems to be defying gravity,” said Niall van de Wouw, chief airfreight officer at logistics analytics firm Xeneta. “The biggest growth driver at the moment is everything related to AI.”

The demand—coupled with higher jet-fuel prices due to the war in Iran—is pushing up rates during what is typically a slow season for airfreight. 

Experts warn there could be pressure on capacity coming.

I talked with International Air Transport Association (IATA), Kuehne+Nagel, DHL Global Forwarding of DHL, DSV - Global Transport and Logistics and others about what they're seeing in the market today and what challenges could lie ahead.

items.content:
The latest edition of Supply Chained is now available.

Trade compliance used to be viewed as a back-office function. Today, it has become a strategic capability.

Tariffs can change overnight. Export controls continue to expand. Sanctions lists are constantly updated. Organizations are expected to know not only what they are shipping, but who is receiving it, how it will be used, and whether the transaction complies with an increasingly complex web of regulations.

In this week's issue, I sit down with Thariq Kara, CEO and co-founder of BITE Data, to discuss how AI is transforming global trade compliance.

▶ The difference between tariffs, export controls, and sanctions
▶ A practical introduction to EAR, ITAR, OFAC, BIS, and other key regulations
▶ The three questions every exporter should ask before shipping a product
▶ Why "deemed exports" matter for universities, research labs, and companies employing international talent
▶ How AI is helping organizations move from manual compliance to intelligent risk detection
▶ Why trade compliance is becoming a source of resilience and competitive advantage

One of the biggest takeaways from our conversation is that AI is not replacing compliance professionals. Instead, it is helping them make better decisions by identifying risks, highlighting gaps, and providing the information needed to navigate an increasingly complex geopolitical environment.

As I discuss in the newsletter, my research defines trust as the choice to accept vulnerability. Better information doesn't eliminate uncertainty, but it helps organizations make better decisions about where they are willing to accept that vulnerability. In many ways, that's what intelligent trade compliance is all about.

What changes have had the biggest impact on your organization's approach to global trade compliance?

items.content:
The latest edition of Supply Chained® is now available.

When most organizations think about waste, they think about disposal. But what if waste isn't actually waste? What if it is simply inventory waiting for a better supply chain?

In this week's issue, I sit down with C.J. Nord, Founder of Supply Chains for Good, to explore how circular supply chains can transform manufacturing waste into energy, valuable materials, and competitive advantage.

▶ Why profitability, not environmental concern alone, will drive the adoption of circular supply chains
▶ The philosophy of "There's cash in that trash" and how waste can become a strategic asset
▶ How biomass reactors convert wood waste into biochar, clean energy, and other high-value products
▶ Why eliminating transportation altogether can be better than optimizing it
▶ How manufacturing facilities could evolve into localized energy-producing microgrids
▶ What biochar teaches us about systems thinking and Supply Chain 5.0

One of my favorite insights from the conversation is that circularity is not simply about recycling. It is about redesigning supply chains so that waste from one process becomes the input for another. When organizations begin viewing waste as inventory instead of disposal, entirely new business models become possible.

The phrase that stayed with me after our conversation was simple: "There's cash in that trash." It perfectly captures the idea that the future of supply chains belongs to organizations that create multiple forms of value from the same resources.

What opportunities are you seeing to make your supply chain more circular?

~Mr. Supply Chain®

items.content:
S&OP. MPS. MRP. CRP.
Four acronyms. One continuous flow from strategy to the shop floor.

Here's how they actually connect:

S&OP — Sales & Operations Plan
Strategic plan. Forecasted vision of sales. This is where you decide the direction — 3 to 18 months out.

MPS — Master Production Schedule
Production scheduling derived from the S&OP. This is where strategy becomes a concrete production plan.

MRP — Material Requirements Planning
Net requirements calculation: gross needs minus existing stock. This is where the plan becomes purchase orders and production orders.

CRP — Capacity Requirements Planning
Real-time workshop and resource management. This is where the plan meets reality machines, people, time.

items.content:
Most companies think S&OP is "the meeting."
It's not. The meeting is just the last 10% of the process.
Here's the full monthly cycle, the 5 steps that actually drive a working S&OP process:

🟢 Step 1 : Data Gathering (1st week of the month)
Sales actuals, supply actuals, statistical forecast. If this step is messy, everything downstream is built on sand.
🟢 Step 2 : Demand Planning
Management forecast. First-pass spreadsheets. This is where the business adjusts the statistics with real market knowledge.
🟢 Step 3 : Supply Planning
Capacity constraints. Second-pass spreadsheets. Now you confront demand with what you can actually deliver.
🟢 Step 4 : Pre-Meeting
Conflict resolution. Recommendations. Agenda for the executive meeting. This is the step most companies skip, and it's the most important one. If conflicts aren't resolved here, they explode in front of the CEO.
🟢 Step 5 : Executive Meeting
Decisions and game plan.
Not a status update. A decision forum.

Most companies run steps 1 to 3 reasonably well.
They fail at step 4. And then step 5 becomes a disaster.

If your executive meeting feels chaotic, look one step back before blaming the meeting itself.

If you’ve ever wondered how much and how often you should order, the EOQ formula (Economic Order Quantity or Wilson Formula) is your answer.
The Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), also known as the Wilson formula, helps you pinpoint the ideal inventory order size.
The goal is to strike a balance between two cost drivers:

👉 Holding Costs: The inventory storage cost increases as the order quantity grows.
👉 Ordering Costs: The transaction cost of placing orders decreases as the order size increases because fewer orders are needed to meet demand.

These costs create two opposing curves.
The Total Cost curve, the sum of Holding and Ordering Costs, reaches its minimum where the two costs are equal.
This intersection represents the EOQ, the optimal order quantity that minimizes total costs.Do you want to implement EOQ?

By 2030, here's where the roles are booming and falling 💥 (US data, but the same trend hits Europe, UK and Asia):

📈 Booming
 🟢 AI & IBP Planning Lead: +80%
 🟢 IBP Director / VP: +65%
 🟢 S&OP / IBP Manager: +45%

📉 Falling
 🔴 Demand Planning Coordinator: -15%
 🔴 Supply Data Analyst: -25%
 🔴 Order Processor: -55%

Same field. Opposite directions.

And the pay follows the green side. A S&OP / IBP Manager now earns around $163k in the US, an IBP Director up to $242k.

So why are these roles exploding? Three reasons:

1️⃣ Volatility is the new normal 🌊

 Before 2020, you could plan once a year in Excel. Not anymore. Shocks, demand swings, tariffs, AI at full speed. S&OP / IBP is the process that realigns demand, supply and finance every month.

2️⃣ AI is moving value from execution to decision 🤖

 AI handles the repetitive stuff: data entry, order processing, basic forecasting. It can't arbitrate between service, cash and capacity when interests collide. That's the human job. So junior roles shrink, decision roles boom.

3️⃣ The profile is rare 🦄

 Business sense AND technical skills, comfortable with the tools, able to lead a room full of people you don't manage. Almost no one has been trained for it. Yet.

If you want to be on the green side of that chart, that's exactly what I teach in the S&OP / IBP Leader program.

items.content:
S&OP is not a process.
 It's the oil that makes your entire business machine run smoothly.
 Look at this visual for a second.
 You have all these gears: CEO, shareholders, clients, sales, suppliers, marketing, product, production, supply chain.
 Each one spinning. Each one with its own priorities, its own pace, its own pressure.
 Without oil, gears grind against each other. Friction. Heat. Eventually, breakdown.
 That's exactly what happens in companies without a real S&OP process.
Sales wants more. Production wants stability. Finance wants efficiency. Everyone optimizes their own gear and the whole machine slows down.
So what's actually in this "oil"?

 Not a tool. Not a template. Not a fancy dashboard.
 The real ingredients are:

Trust. Collaboration. Engagement. Visibility. Process. Tools. Practicality. Optimism.

 Notice something? Only 2 of those 8 ingredients are technical (process, tools).
The other 6 are human.

 That's the part most companies get wrong. They buy the software. They build the template.
And they wonder why the machine still grinds.
 S&OP works when you pour the right oil,not just the right tool.
